walkthroughs.title: Epigastric pain and a black stool

doorway: Presents to the family medicine clinic with stomach pain.
Vital signs are supplied at this station.
A point-of-care hemoglobin was drawn at check-in; the result is on the chart.
Perform a focused history and physical examination, and discuss your plan with the patient.

plan.notice: Black stools with upper abdominal symptoms may represent bleeding; assess current stability and faintness early.
plan.pivot: Clarify tarry versus merely dark stool, vomiting blood, dizziness, NSAID exposure and the actual dose and frequency used.
plan.exam: Assess circulation, pallor and abdomen. A proposed rectal examination is refused under the course SP rules; refusal cannot provide occult-blood or internal findings.
plan.avoid: Documenting a rectal result that was never obtained or treating improvement with acid medication as reassurance against bleeding.

goals: Ask about stool color explicitly. She will not volunteer the black stool - she has already explained it to herself as the iron tablets - and it is the single most important fact in the case.
Ask the dose and frequency of the ibuprofen, not just whether she takes 'anything for pain'. This medication exposure is relevant to the assessment, but it does not establish a diagnosis.
Ask the allergy reaction, not just the allergen. 'Penicillin - swelling' rules out standard triple therapy; 'penicillin - upset stomach' would not.
walkthroughs.variant_guidance: Use this core presentation to learn the sequence before transferring to a variation.

timeline.student: What brings you in today?

timeline.why: Clarify tarry versus merely dark stool, vomiting blood, dizziness, NSAID exposure and the actual dose and frequency used.

timeline.student: How have your symptoms changed since they started?
timeline.patient: It's been creeping up on me, and the last three days it's been a lot worse.
timeline.why: Change over time can change urgency even when the symptom is familiar.

timeline.student: Where do you feel the symptoms?

timeline.student: How bad are the symptoms, and how do they affect what you can do?

timeline.student: Is the pain worse when your stomach is empty or at night?

timeline.student: I recommend emergency evaluation today because the black tarry stool, symptoms and supplied blood count raise concern for bleeding. Ibuprofen can injure the stomach lining. We should stop it and discuss safer pain treatment with the clinician.
timeline.patient: Alright. I can manage that.
timeline.why: Proposed care, not a record of tests or treatment already completed.

timeline.student: What questions do you have about the next steps?
timeline.patient: The black stool - is that bad?

timeline.student: Black tarry stool can represent digested blood, although iron can also darken stool. I recommend urgent evaluation because of the whole history and supplied hemoglobin; we should not assume iron explains it. The team can discuss whether and when endoscopy is needed after assessing stability.
timeline.patient: Thank you for explaining it.
timeline.why: Answer the concern that was just expressed. Give a defensible recommendation and explain uncertainty; do not promise a diagnosis or recovery before the evidence supports it.

note.S:
CC: Burning epigastric pain, 6 weeks; worse for 3 days.
HPI: 29-year-old woman with nonradiating burning/gnawing pain, 7/10 worst and 3/10 between episodes. Worse fasting, at night, with coffee and greater ibuprofen use; brief relief with food/antacids. One black tarry stool 2 days ago; started borrowed iron 1 week ago. Nausea, fatigue for 2–3 weeks and lightheadedness on standing. No hematemesis, coffee-ground emesis, weight loss, dysphagia, jaundice, fever or diarrhea. No prior ulcer. Worried about gastric cancer.
PMH: Chronic knee pain after sports injuries; migraines. PSH: Cholecystectomy at 25; two vaginal deliveries.
Meds: Ibuprofen 800 mg 2–3 times/day for months; ferrous sulfate for 1 week; no PPI. Penicillin causes lip/facial swelling.
SH: School administrator; husband and two children; no tobacco/drugs; 1–2 glasses wine on weekends. FH: Mother died of gastric cancer at 68; father has HTN; sister healthy.
ROS: GI as above; no vomiting. General: fatigue, no fever, night sweats or weight loss. Hematologic: lightheadedness and reported pallor, no bruising, gum bleeding or epistaxis. LMP 2 weeks ago; pregnancy not suspected, not tested.
P: 1. Arrange emergency evaluation today for suspected upper-GI bleeding; obtain CBC, BUN/creatinine, coagulation studies and type/screen, with resuscitation as indicated and GI consultation/endoscopy after stabilization. Stop ibuprofen; clinician-directed acid suppression and alternative analgesia. Explain black tarry stools, hematemesis and syncope as urgent warnings; immediate disposition replaces routine follow-up.

2. GI evaluation and appropriate biopsy at endoscopy if a lesion is identified; investigate H. pylori and tailor treatment to results and penicillin allergy. Explain the purpose of tissue diagnosis and arrange specialist follow-up based on the actual findings.

3. Obtain ferritin, iron studies and reticulocyte count; trend hemoglobin during evaluation. Discuss iron replacement after stabilization and source assessment. Explain that anemia may contribute to fatigue/faintness; defer OMT during acute bleeding.
A: 1. NSAID-induced peptic ulcer disease with upper gastrointestinal bleeding

omissions: Ask about stool color explicitly. She will not volunteer the black stool - she has already explained it to herself as the iron tablets - and it is the single most important fact in the case.
Ask the dose and frequency of the ibuprofen, not just whether she takes 'anything for pain'. This medication exposure is relevant to the assessment, but it does not establish a diagnosis.
Ask the allergy reaction, not just the allergen. 'Penicillin - swelling' rules out standard triple therapy; 'penicillin - upset stomach' would not.
Inspect the conjunctivae. It is thirty seconds and it converts 'she says she is tired' into a documented physical finding.
Auscultate before you percuss or palpate. The hyperactive bowel sounds are a real finding here, and palpating first changes them.

note.S:
CC: Burning epigastric pain, 6 weeks; worse for 3 days.
HPI: 29-year-old woman with nonradiating burning/gnawing pain, 7/10 worst and 3/10 between episodes. Worse fasting, at night, with coffee and greater ibuprofen use; brief relief with food/antacids. One black tarry stool 2 days ago; started borrowed iron 1 week ago. Nausea, fatigue for 2–3 weeks and lightheadedness on standing. No hematemesis, coffee-ground emesis, weight loss, dysphagia, jaundice, fever or diarrhea. No prior ulcer. Worried about gastric cancer.
PMH: Chronic knee pain after sports injuries; migraines. PSH: Cholecystectomy at 25; two vaginal deliveries.
Meds: Ibuprofen 800 mg 2–3 times/day for months; ferrous sulfate for 1 week; no PPI. Penicillin causes lip/facial swelling.
SH: School administrator; husband and two children; no tobacco/drugs; 1–2 glasses wine on weekends. FH: Mother died of gastric cancer at 68; father has HTN; sister healthy.
ROS: GI as above; no vomiting. General: fatigue, no fever, night sweats or weight loss. Hematologic: lightheadedness and reported pallor, no bruising, gum bleeding or epistaxis. LMP 2 weeks ago; pregnancy not suspected, not tested.
Care needs: I am worried about getting to follow-up and knowing whom to call if I get worse.
P: 1. Arrange emergency evaluation today for suspected upper-GI bleeding; obtain CBC, BUN/creatinine, coagulation studies and type/screen, with resuscitation as indicated and GI consultation/endoscopy after stabilization. Stop ibuprofen; clinician-directed acid suppression and alternative analgesia. Explain black tarry stools, hematemesis and syncope as urgent warnings; immediate disposition replaces routine follow-up. Confirm transport and a practical contact for deterioration.

2. GI evaluation and appropriate biopsy at endoscopy if a lesion is identified; investigate H. pylori and tailor treatment to results and penicillin allergy. Explain the purpose of tissue diagnosis and arrange specialist follow-up based on the actual findings.

3. Obtain ferritin, iron studies and reticulocyte count; trend hemoglobin during evaluation. Discuss iron replacement after stabilization and source assessment. Explain that anemia may contribute to fatigue/faintness; defer OMT during acute bleeding.
A: 1. NSAID-induced peptic ulcer disease with upper gastrointestinal bleeding

reasoning.question: Any fainting, ongoing black stools, vomiting blood or inability to keep fluids down?
reasoning.why: Blood-loss severity matters before a routine ulcer plan.
reasoning.if_present: Ongoing bleeding or perfusion symptoms require urgent evaluation.
reasoning.if_absent: Absence of shock symptoms does not make melena a routine delayed follow-up complaint.
reasoning.next_action: Assess vitals, bleeding history, medication risks and safe disposition.

differentials.name: NSAID-induced peptic ulcer disease with upper gastrointestinal bleeding

omissions: Ask about stool color explicitly. She will not volunteer the black stool - she has already explained it to herself as the iron tablets - and it is the single most important fact in the case.
Ask the dose and frequency of the ibuprofen, not just whether she takes 'anything for pain'. This medication exposure is relevant to the assessment, but it does not establish a diagnosis.
Ask the allergy reaction, not just the allergen. 'Penicillin - swelling' rules out standard triple therapy; 'penicillin - upset stomach' would not.
Inspect the conjunctivae. It is thirty seconds and it converts 'she says she is tired' into a documented physical finding.
Auscultate before you percuss or palpate. The hyperactive bowel sounds are a real finding here, and palpating first changes them.

recall.prompt: Before naming a diagnosis, what is the key distinction in this presentation?
recall.answer: Clarify tarry versus merely dark stool, vomiting blood, dizziness, NSAID exposure and the actual dose and frequency used.

recall.prompt: Which specific examination or safety step changes what you can document?
recall.answer: Assess circulation, pallor and abdomen. A proposed rectal examination is refused under the course SP rules; refusal cannot provide occult-blood or internal findings.

recall.prompt: Name one tempting documentation or reasoning error and how you will prevent it.
recall.answer: Documenting a rectal result that was never obtained or treating improvement with acid medication as reassurance against bleeding.
